whyWrong.B: "an explanation" reverses the relationship — the fact explains the difference, not the other way around.
whyWrong.C: "a repudiation" means a rejection, but the speed gap does not deny the fact; it follows from it.
whyWrong.D: "an objective" would make the speed difference a goal someone aimed at, which makes no sense for animal anatomy.

commonMistakes: Cause-and-effect blanks are easy to invert; name which half is the cause before choosing.

whyCorrect: The colon spells out what the blank means: a "constantly evolving network of channels and strips of land that change in size and shape" as sediment is deposited. A system in constant change is dynamic, so that is the word the blank needs.

whyWrong.B: "sustainable" is about being able to continue without depleting resources, which the text never addresses.
whyWrong.C: "immutable" means unchanging, the exact opposite of a delta that is constantly evolving.
whyWrong.D: "unrivaled" means unmatched by any other, but the sentence opens with "As with other river deltas," placing this delta among its peers rather than above them.

tips: Read the words after the colon before looking at the choices — they define the blank outright.

whyCorrect: The clause after the colon gives the rule: no two minor planets may share a name. A name that no other body can have is one that belongs to that body alone, so the blank must mean unique to it.

whyWrong.B: "evocative of" would require the name to call the body to mind, but the stated rule is about uniqueness, not suggestiveness.
whyWrong.C: "typical for" would mean the name is ordinary for such a body, which is unrelated to the no-duplicates rule.
whyWrong.D: "superseded by" means replaced by, which reverses the relationship between name and object entirely.

commonMistakes: The naming of 1061 Paeonia after peonies tempts students toward a word about evocative naming, but the colon points to the uniqueness rule instead.

whyCorrect: The two terms appear in a list of things different studies emphasize, and the sentence ends by saying walking decisions are made in complex contexts where multiple conditions and needs matter. So each named factor is real but partial — one contributor among many that any single study tends to foreground.

whyWrong.A: Alfonzo's point is that our understanding is not robust enough, not that these particular factors have been overstated, and the text does not assert they drive most people's decisions.
whyWrong.B: The text never limits these factors to Copenhagen; Copenhagen is the example of a city whose features may not transfer elsewhere.
whyWrong.C: The text does not claim people rarely consider these things — it claims they are not the whole picture.

tips: When examples appear in a list ending with "and so on," they usually illustrate incompleteness rather than error.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences describe the exhibition: thirty North Carolina artists across a range of disciplines, from painting to sculpture. The last sentence turns to what makes it unusual for the Nasher specifically — it borrows many works, while the museum normally builds shows around its own permanent collection. Overview, then the departure from institutional practice.

whyWrong.A: The comparison is with the Nasher's own usual practice, not with exhibitions generally, and the text never analyzes what that difference means.
whyWrong.B: The curators' goals are never stated, and no evaluation of their success appears.
whyWrong.D: The range of disciplines is only one sentence of setup, and the text never explains why those disciplines were included.

commonMistakes: Structure choices often fail on their second half; check that the text really does the analyzing or evaluating a choice claims.

whyCorrect: The text reports the gap in park use — 82.9% in Quito against 69.9% in Buenos Aires — and then rules out one explanation for it. Quito residents reported much less access to other desired amenities near parks, so better nearby amenities cannot be why more of them use parks. The main idea is the finding plus that ruled-out explanation.

whyWrong.A: The text says nothing about how many parks each city has.
whyWrong.B: No prediction about adding amenities is made; the text only rules out amenities as the explanation for the existing gap.
whyWrong.D: It reverses the reported comparison and adds a claim about overall amenity counts that the text never makes.

tips: When a text ends by eliminating an explanation, that elimination is usually the main idea, not a side remark.

whyCorrect: The text sets up an assumption — many researchers grouped cuttlefish with octopuses and squid as lacking 3D vision — and then reports a test of it. Cuttlefish in 3D glasses adjusted their strike position to match projected 3D shrimp, which suggests their vision resembles that of horses and barn owls instead. The main idea is that the old assumption looks wrong.

whyWrong.A: Horses and barn owls are only the reference point for 3D vision; the text's subject is cuttlefish.
whyWrong.B: The finding pushes cuttlefish away from octopuses and squid, and the text discusses vision rather than body structure.
whyWrong.D: The text mentions perceiving distance and depth, not interaction between animals, and it makes no general claim about many species.

tips: When a text says researchers "once thought" something and then describes a test, the main idea is almost always the overturning of that belief.

whyCorrect: Trace each word's path. "Cocoa" travelled from Nahuatl to Spanish to English, and "iguana" travelled from Taino to Spanish to English. In both cases Spanish is the middle step through which an Indigenous word reached English. That is the point the author makes about Spanish: it acted as the route.

whyWrong.B: No counts or totals of any language's contribution to English are given, so no comparison of scale is possible.
whyWrong.C: The text shows Spanish borrowing from Indigenous languages but never shows it giving words to them.
whyWrong.D: The text mentions one Nahuatl word and one Taino word as examples, which says nothing about how many words Spanish adopted from each.

commonMistakes: Two examples are enough to establish a pattern but never enough to support a claim about quantities — treat any choice with "equally" or "more" as suspect.

whyCorrect: Match the conclusion to the rating that measures it. The conclusion is about how well the methodology was explained, and traceability is defined as the rating for clearer description of procedures — consistency measures something else entirely, how well the material categories line up with the database. So the conclusion is challenged by Huisman scoring lower than Oguchi on traceability.

whyWrong.B: High ratings on both scales for Huisman support the conclusion rather than challenging it.
whyWrong.C: Consistency measures category alignment, not clarity of procedure, so a lower consistency rating leaves the methodology claim untouched.
whyWrong.D: Low ratings for Oguchi would strengthen the claim that Huisman explained the methodology better.

tips: When a text defines two separate measures, find which one the conclusion actually depends on before evaluating any finding.

whyCorrect: The worry was that virtual tours would replace in-person visits. The administrators say that worry was unfounded, so support has to show virtual tours leading to visits rather than away from them. Surveyed visitors saying the virtual tours convinced them to plan an in-person visit is exactly that.

whyWrong.A: Where visitors live says nothing about whether virtual tours discouraged anyone from coming.
whyWrong.C: Viewing tours afterward to reminisce shows the tours do not replace a visit already made, but it does not address whether they deter people from visiting in the first place.
whyWrong.D: If most visitors had never heard of the virtual tours, the tours could not have influenced their decision either way, so this leaves the concern untested.

commonMistakes: Support has to bear on the direction of the concern — a fact that is merely compatible with the claim is not evidence for it.

whyCorrect: The claim names two things at once: attention given to humanitarian causes abroad and neglect of suffering close to home. This quotation contains both. "When ye plead for the wrecked and fallen, / The exile from far-distant shores" is the distant cause, and "Remember that men are still wasting / Life's crimson around your own doors" is the reproach for overlooking what is happening locally.

whyWrong.A: It is a prayer for the speaker's own country and never mentions attention directed abroad, so no misplaced focus is being criticized.
whyWrong.B: It promises that divine justice will eventually reach those who oppress the poor, which is about retribution rather than about where activists direct their efforts.
whyWrong.C: It praises the present age for people of different creeds working together, which offers no criticism at all.

tips: For a two-part claim, check each quotation for both parts; the one that names the foreign cause and the local neglect in the same lines is the answer.

whyCorrect: The passage pairs region of origin with neighborhood. Immigrants from north China, where Mandarin dominates, cluster in Flushing and speak Mandarin; immigrants from south China, where Cantonese and Fuzhounese are common, cluster in Chinatown and speak those. The neighborhood language pattern is simply the language map of China carried over by where people settled.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text concerns how many languages any immigrant speaks or how arrival date affects that.
whyWrong.C: Frequent moving between boroughs would blur the neighborhood pattern the text describes, not produce it.
whyWrong.D: The text gives no population figures, so no claim about which group is larger can be drawn — and group size would not explain why the two neighborhoods differ.

tips: When a text lays out a parallel between two places of origin and two destinations, the explanation is usually that the origin pattern was carried to the destination.
